## #788 closed — and the shape changed

The fix that shipped isn't the one the issue proposed. #788 asked to cache the last-known `is_workspace_admin` across a throttled refetch; I built that first, and the path **doesn't exist** — after a successful load `MeProvider` only refetches via a timer a 429 itself sets, so a cached `ok` is never the state a later 429 lands on. That's the session's recurring lesson from a new angle: not a test that proves nothing, but a test whose *failure output lies about what broke*.

- **#1023** — both Airflow connections failing **every poll for ~47 hours**. - **#925** — assets paging past the 200-row cap plus honest dashboard truncation. The largest of the batch.

content.text: My #1023 diagnosis was **wrong**, and I need to correct it before anyone acts on it. The harness Airflow is `Stopped` — deliberately, per the 2026-07-04 cost wind-down — and ACA's ingress returns 404 for a stopped app. It is not an Airflow 2-vs-3 API path problem at all:

input.command:
gh issue edit 1023 --title "airflow: a stopped provider reports as 'check your connection config' — misleading classification, not an outage" 2>&1|tail -1
gh issue comment 1023 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Correcting my own root cause — the Airflow 2/3 API theory is wrong

I filed this claiming the harness Airflow had moved to Airflow 3 and our poller was still on `/api/v1/`. **That is not what is happening.** Verified:

```
az containerapp list --query "[?contains(name,'airflow')]..."
dataq-harness-airflow           dataq-rg   Stopped   1
dataq-harness-airflow-worker    dataq-rg   Stopped   2
dataq-harness-airflow-trigger   dataq-rg   Stopped   1
```

The harness Airflow is **deliberately stopped** — the 2026-07-04 Azure cost wind-down (#590) leaves harness compute off by default. Azure Container Apps' ingress serves an `Azure Container App - Unavailable` page for a stopped app, and that page comes back **404**. Our poller sees a 404 and there is nothing wrong with our API path.

I reached the wrong conclusion by reasoning from the status code and the URL shape without checking whether the host was even up. `/api/v2/version` returns the same Azure error page, which would have told me immediately.

## What is actually left here

Two things, both smaller than the original claim, and neither an outage:

1. **The classified reason is misleading.** `last_poll_error` says *"The connection or run target looks misconfigured — e.g. a missing warehouse or role, or a table/path that does not exist. Check the connection and the suite's run target."* Nothing is wrong with the connection config; the host is down. A 404 whose body is an infrastructure error page is a reachability signal, not a user misconfiguration, and the advice sends an operator to the wrong place. (#605's classifier keys on substrings, and "not found" lands in CONFIG.)

2. **An intentionally-stopped integration accumulates unbounded failures and — since #842/#843 shipped — will now alert.** That may be correct behaviour (DataQ genuinely cannot reach the provider) or it may be noise we should be able to silence per connection. Worth a decision rather than a default.

## Revised acceptance criteria

## I got #1023 wrong, and corrected it

I filed it claiming the harness Airflow had upgraded to Airflow 3 and our poller was stuck on `/api/v1/`. That was confidently wrong.

Corrected in both places it had spread: the issue (retitled, rescoped, with the withdrawn AC struck) and `docs/progress.md`, which had recorded the wrong cause as fact. Leaving that standing was the real risk — someone would have spent a day migrating an API that doesn't need migrating.

That's the substantive finding. DataQ is behaving correctly: an integration it genuinely cannot reach is reported as failing. What survives from #1023 is smaller and real:

1. **The classified reason misleads.** It tells the operator to check a connection config that's fine, when the signal is that the host is unreachable. #605's classifier keys on substrings and "not found" lands in CONFIG.
2. **A deliberately-offline integration accumulates unbounded failures and now alerts** (since #842/#843 shipped in this deploy). That wants a decision — mutable per connection, or accepted as correct — not a default.

- **#1023's fix** — distinguishing an unreachable-host 4xx/5xx from a genuine missing-resource 404. Harder than it looks: a 404 from an HTTP provider is genuinely ambiguous, and keying on Azure's error page would bake in exactly the cloud lock-in ADR 0010/0013 forbids. Needs a real design decision.
- **#1024** — credential expiry inert for up to 24h after a deploy, and `NULL` now conflating "no readable expiry" with "haven't looked yet".

# Ops log — harness lifecycle + credential rotation

Append-only record of two things that are **invisible in code and expensive to
reconstruct**: when harness compute was started or stopped, and when a credential
was rotated and when it next expires.

## Why this file exists, and why it is git-tracked

On 2026-07-26 both prod Airflow connections showed ~280 consecutive poll failures.
Working out whether that was an incident or an intentionally-stopped harness took
several Azure queries, and I still got the attribution wrong twice — first
inventing an Airflow-3 API migration, then citing the wrong shutdown date. The
answer existed only as a `systemData.lastModifiedAt` timestamp on a Container App.

The harness repo (ADR 0021) is deliberately **not** git-tracked, so a log kept
there has no history, no review, and no diff. The whole value of this record is
history — which is what git is for. So it lives here, in the tracked repo, even
though it describes external infrastructure.

The same shape burned us before on credentials: one credential is copied into **N
per-connection Key Vault secrets**, and rotating some but not all left two
Snowflake connections silently dead for three weeks (root-caused 2026-07-25).
A rotation entry that lists *every* derived secret is the countermeasure.

## Rules

1. **Never record a secret value.** Identifiers, dates and owners only. A name
   like `conn-snowflake-retail` is a Key Vault *key*, not a credential — the
   value never appears here, in any form, redacted or otherwise.
2. **Absolute dates, always** (`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC`). "Yesterday" is useless in
   six weeks, and this file exists to be read cold.
3. **Say who and why.** "Stopped" answers almost nothing; "stopped, cost
   wind-down, expected down until the next test window" answers the question that
   actually gets asked.
4. **Rotating one credential means rotating every secret derived from it.** List
   them all in the entry, so a partial rotation is visible as a short list rather
   than discovered weeks later.
5. **Append; never rewrite history.** A wrong entry gets a correcting entry
   beneath it, the way [#1023](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1023)
   got a correction rather than a quiet edit.

---

## Harness lifecycle

Harness compute is **stopped by default** since the 2026-07-04 cost wind-down
(#590) — roughly CAD 17/day awake versus ~0 stopped. `harness_window.sh` opens a
test window (wake → run the flows → sleep again). Anything left running outside a
window is either deliberate or a mistake, and this log is how the two are told
apart.

| When (UTC) | Service | Action | By | Why / expected state |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-07-18 19:36 | `dataq-harness-airflow` (+ `-worker`, `-trigger`) | **Stopped** | royarijit04@outlook.com | Verified from `systemData.lastModifiedAt` on 2026-07-26, not from memory. Intentional. Consequence, now understood: DataQ polls it every 10 min, ACA's ingress answers 404 for a stopped app, and the connection accumulates failures — 282 by 2026-07-26. Expected to stay down until a test window needs Airflow. |
| 2026-07-26 06:16 | `dataq-app-{api,worker,frontend}` | Deployed `c401572d` | Deploy workflow | App stack, not harness. Recorded here because the roll restarted the worker and reset in-memory state. |

> **Unresolved as of 2026-07-26:** 282 failures at a 10-minute cadence is ~47h,
> but the app has been stopped since 2026-07-18 (~192h) — about a quarter of the
> expected count. Either beat is not ticking at its scheduled rate (see
> [#905](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/905)), the counter does
> not increment on every attempt, or something reset the streak. Not yet
> diagnosed; `pipeline_runs` + `connections.last_polled_at` in the prod DB would
> settle it.

---

## Credential rotation

One credential typically becomes **several** Key Vault secrets — one per
connection that uses it. The "Secrets written" column must list every one, or the
next reader cannot tell a complete rotation from a partial one.

| Rotated (UTC) | Credential | Secrets written | Expires | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-07-05 | Snowflake `DATAQ_READER` / `DATAQ_LOADER` PATs | `conn-snowflake-retail` only | — | **Partial — this is the incident.** `conn-snowflake-orders` and `conn-snowflake-payments` were left on the 2026-06-28 value and stayed dead until 2026-07-25. Logged retrospectively as the worked example of why this table has a "Secrets written" column. |
| 2026-07-25 | Snowflake `DATAQ_READER` / `DATAQ_LOADER` PATs | `conn-snowflake-retail`, `conn-snowflake-orders`, `conn-snowflake-payments` | **2026-07-29** | All three verified with a connection test after writing. `SecretStore` reads Key Vault at runtime, so **no container restart is needed** — the opposite of env-injected secrets. |

### Expiring soon

Keep this ordered by date. It is the one part of the file worth reading at a
glance, and #838's automated warning does **not** cover these — a Snowflake PAT
carries no readable expiry, so the product cannot know it (and
[#1024](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1024) notes the SAS case
is inert for up to 24h after a deploy). Until that changes, this table is the
only warning.

| Expires | Credential | Action needed |
|---|---|---|
| **2026-07-29** | Snowflake `DATAQ_READER` / `DATAQ_LOADER` PATs | Re-mint and write **all three** `conn-snowflake-*` secrets, then test each connection. |
| unknown | ADLS SAS (`conn-adls-*`), Databricks PAT (`conn-unity-catalog-*`) | Expiry not recorded — capture it at the next rotation. A SAS carries `se=` in the token, so #838 can read it once the sweep runs. |

"""Add a PostToolUse:Bash hook reminding that docs/ops-log.md must be updated.

Matches the repo's existing `gh pr merge` → progress.md reminder exactly in shape:
read the tool input, grep the command, emit `additionalContext` when it matches.
"""

import json
import pathlib

MSG = (
    "Harness/credential state just changed - append an entry to docs/ops-log.md NOW "
    "(it is append-only and git-tracked on purpose). Harness start/stop: record UTC "
    "timestamp, the service(s), the action, who, and the EXPECTED state afterwards - "
    "'stopped' alone does not answer the question that gets asked later ('was this "
    "deliberate?'), which cost real time on 2026-07-26. Credential rotation: record "
    "the rotation date, the credential, EVERY Key Vault secret written from it, and "
    "the new expiry - a partial rotation left two Snowflake connections dead for "
    "three weeks. Never record a secret VALUE, only identifiers and dates."
)

# Harness lifecycle: az containerapp start/stop (incl. `job`), scale-to-zero via
# min-replicas, and the harness window script. Credential rotation: writing a Key
# Vault secret, or DataQ's own reauth endpoint.
PATTERN = (
    r"(az[[:space:]]+containerapp([[:space:]]+job)?[[:space:]]+(start|stop)"
    r"|az[[:space:]]+containerapp[[:space:]]+update.*--min-replicas"
    r"|harness_window\.sh"
    r"|az[[:space:]]+keyvault[[:space:]]+secret[[:space:]]+set"
    r"|/connections/[^[:space:]]*/reauth)"
)

COMMAND = (
    "input=$(cat); "
    "cmd=$(printf '%s' \"$input\" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty'); "
    f"if printf '%s' \"$cmd\" | grep -Eq '{PATTERN}'; then "
    "printf '%s' '"
    + json.dumps(
        {
            "hookSpecificOutput": {
                "hookEventName": "PostToolUse",
                "additionalContext": MSG,
            }
        }
    )
    + "'; fi"
)

p = pathlib.Path(".claude/settings.json")
settings = json.loads(p.read_text())

for entry in settings["hooks"]["PostToolUse"]:
    if entry.get("matcher") == "Bash":
        cmds = [h.get("command", "") for h in entry["hooks"]]
        if any("ops-log.md" in c for c in cmds):
            print("already present - no change")
            break
        entry["hooks"].append({"type": "command", "command": COMMAND})
        p.write_text(json.dumps(settings, indent=2) + "\n")
        print(f"hook added; PostToolUse:Bash now has {len(entry['hooks'])} hooks")
        break
else:
    raise SystemExit("no PostToolUse:Bash matcher found")

The hook just fired on my own **commit message** — because that message *mentions* `harness_window.sh`. That's a false positive, and a serious one: a hook that cries wolf every time someone writes about the harness gets ignored, and an ignored hook is worse than none.

The pattern matches anywhere in the string. It needs to match the command being **invoked**:

input.content:
"""Re-anchor the ops-log hook so it matches an INVOKED command, not any mention.

The first version grepped the whole command string, so writing *about* the harness
— a commit message, a grep, a doc edit — tripped it. A reminder that fires when
nothing happened is one people learn to dismiss, which costs more than never
having added it.

Fix: split the command on shell separators and require a trigger at the START of a
segment. A commit message lives inside a segment beginning `git commit`, so it no
longer matches, while a real `... && az containerapp stop ...` still does.
"""

import json
import pathlib

MSG = (
    "Harness/credential state just changed - append an entry to docs/ops-log.md NOW "
    "(append-only, git-tracked on purpose). Harness start/stop: record UTC timestamp, "
    "the service(s), the action, who, and the EXPECTED state afterwards - 'stopped' "
    "alone does not answer the question asked later ('was this deliberate?'), which "
    "cost real time on 2026-07-26. Credential rotation: record the date, the "
    "credential, EVERY Key Vault secret written from it, and the new expiry - a "
    "partial rotation left two Snowflake connections dead for three weeks. Never "
    "record a secret VALUE, only identifiers and dates."
)

# Anchored at ^ of each segment (see module docstring).
PATTERN = (
    r"^(az[[:space:]]+containerapp([[:space:]]+job)?[[:space:]]+(start|stop)"
    r"|az[[:space:]]+containerapp[[:space:]]+update([[:space:]].*)?--min-replicas"
    r"|az[[:space:]]+keyvault[[:space:]]+secret[[:space:]]+set"
    r"|([^[:space:]]*/)?harness_window\.sh)"
)

COMMAND = (
    "input=$(cat); "
    "cmd=$(printf '%s' \"$input\" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty'); "
    # Split on shell separators, strip leading whitespace, then anchor the match so
    # only an invoked command counts - not a mention inside a message or a grep.
    "if printf '%s' \"$cmd\" | tr '\\n;&|' '\\n\\n\\n\\n' | sed 's/^[[:space:]]*//' "
    f"| grep -Eq '{PATTERN}'; then "
    "printf '%s' '"
    + json.dumps(
        {
            "hookSpecificOutput": {
                "hookEventName": "PostToolUse",
                "additionalContext": MSG,
            }
        }
    )
    + "'; fi"
)

p = pathlib.Path(".claude/settings.json")
settings = json.loads(p.read_text())
for entry in settings["hooks"]["PostToolUse"]:
    if entry.get("matcher") == "Bash":
        for h in entry["hooks"]:
            if "ops-log.md" in h.get("command", ""):
                h["command"] = COMMAND
                p.write_text(json.dumps(settings, indent=2) + "\n")
                print("hook re-anchored")
                raise SystemExit(0)
raise SystemExit("ops-log hook not found")

**No — keep it. It's not stale, it holds an open blocker.**

And it answers the question I couldn't close earlier. The file is dated **2026-07-18**, the same day Airflow was stopped at 19:36:

- Snowflake Enterprise began **enforcing MFA on password logins**, killing every password-auth harness leg (`dbt-lineage` failed at 19:21Z with `250001 (08001)`, `flow_a_snowflake_load` presumed dead). DataQ's own connection was unaffected — it uses PAT auth.
- Partially fixed same day: a loader PAT works (dbt build PASS=14).
- **Still open:** the `on-run-end` GRANT hook fails — `DATAQ_LOADER must have MANAGE GRANTS` (42501). Needs a one-time Snowsight grant; 1 model ERROR / 2 SKIP are likely downstream.

So the harness was stopped *right after* that session hit a wall — which is the "why" my ops-log entry was missing.

The file itself is the right place for harness-side working notes. But that residual is a real open item living only in an **untracked, unbacked-up file** — exactly the evaporation risk we just built the log to fix:

Promoted from `HARNESS_TODO.md` (2026-07-18), which is **untracked and unbacked-up** — this item existed in exactly one file on one machine.

## Context

On 2026-07-18 the Snowflake Enterprise account began enforcing **MFA on password logins**, which killed every password-auth harness leg: the `--dbt` window's `dbt-lineage` job failed at 19:21Z with

```
250001 (08001): Failed to authenticate: MFA authentication is required,
but none of your current MFA methods...
```

and `flow_a_snowflake_load` (same password env) is presumed equally dead. **DataQ's own connections were unaffected** — they authenticate with PATs.

That was resolved the same day by minting a loader PAT: `dbt build` PASS=14 as `ROYARIJIT04` + `DATAQ_LOADER`.

## What's still open

The dbt `on-run-end` GRANT hook fails:

```
42501: DATAQ_LOADER must have MANAGE GRANTS
```

`DATAQ_LOADER` owns neither the `ANALYTICS_STG` nor `ANALYTICS` schema, and doesn't hold `MANAGE GRANTS`. One model ERROR and two SKIPs are likely downstream of this.

## Fix (one-time, needs Snowsight — programmatic admin is MFA-walled)

Either:

```sql
GRANT OWNERSHIP ON SCHEMA DATAQ_DB.ANALYTICS_STG TO ROLE DATAQ_LOADER COPY CURRENT GRANTS;
GRANT OWNERSHIP ON SCHEMA DATAQ_DB.ANALYTICS   TO ROLE DATAQ_LOADER COPY CURRENT GRANTS;
```

or pre-create FUTURE grants to `DATAQ_READER` and delete the hook entirely.

Then re-run a `--dbt` window to confirm fully green.

## Why this matters beyond the harness

The `--dbt` window is what generates real table→table DML in Snowflake, and that is what lights up **column-level lineage** in DataQ (pairs flow automatically via the daily refresh once `ACCOUNT_USAGE` has it). So this blocks live verification of the lineage path, not just a harness build.

## Related

#609 (the dbt lineage harness project), [docs/ops-log.md](../blob/main/docs/ops-log.md) (harness lifecycle — the 2026-07-18 stop happened right after this session hit the wall).

content.text:
#1023 closed as not-planned, with the reasoning recorded rather than a bare close.

## What #1024 needs to close

One thing: **make `NULL` mean one thing instead of two.** Right now it means both "this credential type has no readable expiry" (a Snowflake PAT — correctly unknowable) and "we haven't looked yet". The cold-start fix shrank the second window to seconds but didn't remove the ambiguity.

The cheap fix is a `credential_expiry_checked_at` column, stamped on **every** refresh attempt regardless of outcome:

| `checked_at` | `expires_at` | means |
|---|---|---|
| NULL | NULL | never looked — say nothing |
| set | NULL | looked; this credential states no expiry — correct silence |
| set | set | warn inside the window |

Additive nullable column, so no two-step deploy. Then service + API field + UI copy + tests. Roughly one PR.

## The plan

61 open issues; you've named ~17. Sequenced by **dependency and risk**, not issue number:

**1 — Security first: #989.** `SafeMonitorError` echoes a target cell value, which its own rule forbids. A leak that our own declared-safe mechanism permits outranks everything else here.

**2 — The connection-health cluster (one area, interlocking).** In this order because each depends on the last:
- **#998** — health conflates a broken *suite* with a dead *connection*. Semantics first.
- **#999** — ranks the full run history per connection on every page load; needs the index, which collides with single-transaction migrations (settle with #748).
- **#1024** second half — the `checked_at` column above.
- **#996** — alerting on the streak. **Must come last**: alerting on wrong semantics is far worse than badging on them, and I flagged exactly that on the issue.

**3 — Seam refactors, cheap and de-risking.** #727 (`run_target` duplicates dispatch-by-type outside `ConnectionAdapter`), #682 (webhook-auth metadata onto the provider). Both are "move logic behind the abstraction that already exists".

**4 — #936.** Dialect threaded into `core_table`. Contained but a real signature change — both call sites build the clause before a connection exists.

**5 — Ops reliability.** #748 (migration `lock_timeout` + retry) then #905 (worker wedged, beat never ticked). #748 first because #999's index fix depends on how we settle it.

**6 — The big ones, last.** #925 (assets paging), #919 (catalog sync), #912 (Snowpark stitching), #892 (GET_LINEAGE traversal). Each is feature-sized.

**7 — Harness.** #1032 I can do — it's Terraform plus the dbt profile. **#1030 is blocked on you**: it needs a Snowsight grant, and programmatic admin is MFA-walled.

Two notes before I start. **#685** (purge/redact path for connection version history) isn't in your list but is the same immutability-vs-deletion shape as #372 — worth folding in if you want it. And realistically the group of four in step 6 is where this stops being a burn-down and becomes feature work; I'd rather flag that now than discover it at issue fifteen.

Starting on #989.

Found by the agentic review on [#986](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/986) (the #900 fix). Documented in the code at the time but **not filed** — filed now under CONTRIBUTING rule 3a, since a limitation that lives only in a docstring is folklore, not tracked work.

## The inconsistency

`#900` established the rule that a monitor's `error_message` is persisted verbatim **only** when the exception is marked `SafeMonitorError`, and the marker's docstring defines the bar as:

> Subclass this **only** when every message the exception can carry is built by DataQ from the user's own configuration (a column name, a numeric range, a monitor kind) or from static text.

`_as_aware_datetime` (`backend/app/datasources/monitors.py`) does not meet that bar:

```python
raise MonitorConfigError(
    f"freshness value from {source} is not a parseable timestamp: {scalar[:40]!r}"
)
```

`scalar` is a **cell value read from the target table** — data, not configuration. `MonitorConfigError` is safe-marked, so this string is persisted verbatim into `results.observed_value` and rendered in the UI.

## Why it is not a live leak

Stated so nobody escalates this beyond its actual severity:

- It is a **freshness column's** value, so by construction the data is a timestamp-ish column — not a credential, not free-text PII.
- The same column's value is already returned as `observed_value` on the **success** path, so a reader of that check can see it anyway. This discloses nothing new to that audience.
- It is truncated to 40 characters.

So the exposure is bounded and arguably justified — you cannot tell a user *which* value is unparseable without showing it. The docstring now says so explicitly.

## Why it is still worth an issue

1. **The invariant is stated more strictly than it is enforced.** The next person adding a `SafeMonitorError` subclass reads a rule that the codebase itself already breaks, which erodes the rule. Either the rule widens (with the widening argued) or this call site changes.
2. **The redaction policy has no say here.** Suites carry a column policy (`column_policy`, #417/#365) that governs failing-sample redaction. This path bypasses it entirely — if a user ever points a freshness monitor at a column they consider sensitive, the redaction machinery that exists for exactly that purpose is not consulted.
3. It is the kind of narrow, reasoned exception that becomes a precedent by accident.

## Options

- **(a)** Drop the value entirely: "…is not a parseable timestamp" plus the column name. Loses diagnosability; the user must query the column themselves.
- **(b)** Keep it, and widen the marker's rule to "config, static text, or a bounded echo of the value under test — justified per site". Honest, but weakens the guarantee.
- **(c)** Route the echo through the suite's column policy, so a column marked sensitive is masked here exactly as it would be in a failing sample. Most consistent with the rest of the product; most work.

(c) is the one that makes the two redaction stories agree.

## Acceptance criteria

Make `NULL` mean one thing instead of two. A `credential_expiry_checked_at` column, stamped on **every** refresh attempt regardless of outcome:

| `checked_at` | `expires_at` | means |
|---|---|---|
| NULL | NULL | never looked — say nothing |

gh issue comment 989 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Design for (c), refined — and the seam problem it has to avoid

Reading `run_service._redact_row` settles what the rule should be. For the **tested** column it is:

```python
show = not _known_sensitive(name, vals, policy, tags)
```

That is exactly right for a freshness column: echo the cell unless the column is *known* sensitive. Same rule, same policy, same classifier — which is the consistency this issue is asking for.

**But `_known_sensitive` cannot be called from where the leak is.** It lives in `services/run_service.py`, and the leak is in `datasources/monitors.py`. `datasources/` is deliberately decoupled from `services/` (it takes primitives, never the ORM, never service code) — importing upward would invert that dependency to fix a redaction bug, which trades a bounded echo for a structural regression. Not worth it.

**So pass a callable, not a policy.** The caller builds the masker; `datasources/` stays ignorant of what a policy even looks like:

```python
# datasources/monitors.py
def run_monitor_specs(scalar_for, *, monitors, now,
                      mask_value: Callable[[str, Any], Any] | None = None): ...

# the leak site, now:
shown = mask_value(column, scalar) if mask_value else scalar
raise MonitorConfigError(f"freshness value from {source} is not a parseable timestamp: {shown!r}")
```

Surface: the `MonitorRunner` protocol gains an optional `mask_value`, its three implementations (SQL, flat-file, Iceberg) thread it to `run_monitor_specs`, and `worker/tasks.py` — which already holds `column_policy` — builds it from the suite's policy + tags via the existing `_known_sensitive`. Default `None` keeps every current caller and test working unchanged.

**Why a callable rather than widening `MonitorSpec`:** the policy is a *run* concern, not a *monitor definition* concern. Putting it on the spec would persist a redaction decision into check config, where it would drift from the suite's policy the moment that policy changed.

Two things to get right when implementing:

1. **The truncation must stay outside the mask.** Masking first, then `[:40]`, can slice a mask token into something that looks like data. Truncate the *shown* value last.
2. **A test with a sensitive column must assert the value is absent from `results.observed_value`** — not merely that the mask function was called. The failure mode here is a message that gets persisted, so assert on the persisted text.
EOF

    *,
    tested_column: str | None = None,

    tags: Mapping[str, str] | None = None,

    """Redact a result's `sample_failures` for safe surfacing on the read API.

    `sample_failures` carries aggregate counts plus `partial_unexpected_list` — the
    failing values of the **tested column** — and (when the runner records it) an
    `unexpected_index_list` of failing rows. Suite-level ``view`` authz lets
    share-recipients read a suite's results, so PII must not cross that boundary
    unredacted (CLAUDE.md PII rule; purged on the retention sweep below).

    Column-aware policy (#415) — surgical, not blanket, over three authority layers:
    datasource **tags** (``tags``, a governance floor — later increment), the suite
    **override** (``policy``), and the name+value **classifier**. Rules:

    * numeric summary keys (`unexpected_count` / `unexpected_percent`) always pass;
    * `partial_unexpected_list` (the tested column's scalar failing values) passes when

      PII + unclassified masked;

def test_redact_observed_value_passes_through_when_there_is_no_cell() -> None:

def test_redact_observed_value_shows_a_non_sensitive_cell() -> None:
    """The diagnostic is the whole point: "your timestamp column has junk in it" is
    unactionable without the junk. A freshness column is the analogue of the tested
    column in a failing sample, so it shows unless *known* sensitive."""
    out = run_service.redact_observed_value(
        {"error": "…not a parseable timestamp", "unparsed_value": "13/07/2026", "column": "order_ts"}
    )
    assert out is not None and out["unparsed_value"] == "13/07/2026"


def test_redact_observed_value_masks_a_policy_pii_cell() -> None:
    """The case #989 exists for. Before this, a freshness monitor pointed at a
    column the user had declared PII echoed that column's value into
    `results.observed_value` and out to the UI, alerts and MCP — bypassing the
    redaction machinery that exists for exactly this."""
    out = run_service.redact_observed_value(
        {"unparsed_value": "not-a-date", "column": "email"},
        policy={"pii_columns": ["email"]},
    )
    assert out is not None and out["unparsed_value"] != "not-a-date"


def test_redact_observed_value_masks_on_a_governance_tag_too() -> None:
    """Tags are the floor authority — a datasource-tagged column masks even with no
    suite policy set, matching `redact_sample_failures`."""
    out = run_service.redact_observed_value(
        {"unparsed_value": "not-a-date", "column": "ssn"},
        tags={"ssn": "pii"},
    )

def test_redact_observed_value_masks_when_the_column_is_unknown() -> None:

    show the cell. Fail closed — the same default the sample path takes when it has
    no tested-column context."""
    out = run_service.redact_observed_value({"unparsed_value": "not-a-date", "column": None})

git checkout -qb fix/issue-989-monitor-cell-redaction && git add -A && git status --short && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
fix(monitors): stop echoing a target cell in a safe-marked error message

Fixes #989. Option (c) — route the echo through the suite's column policy.

`_as_aware_datetime` interpolated the offending cell into a `MonitorConfigError`
message. That message is safe-marked, so it persists VERBATIM into
`results.observed_value` and renders in the UI, alerts and MCP output — none of
which consult the suite's column policy. A freshness monitor pointed at a column
the user had declared PII echoed that column's value straight past the redaction
machinery that exists for exactly this.

It also made the marker's own rule false. `SafeMonitorError` says to subclass it
only when every message is built from config or static text; this call site broke
that, and a rule the codebase itself breaks is a rule that erodes.

**Implemented at the READ layer, not by threading a policy into `datasources/`.**
The original sketch was to pass the policy down to the leak site. Reading
`redact_sample_failures` showed the product already solves this the other way:
samples are stored raw and masked at the three read boundaries (`api/v1/runs.py`,
`mcp/server.py`, `alerting/builder.py`), which keeps `datasources/` ignorant of
what a policy is. Threading one down would have inverted that dependency to fix a
redaction bug.

So the message is now value-free by construction and the cell travels
structurally on `MonitorConfigError.unparsed_value`, landing in `observed_value`
where the new `redact_observed_value` masks it under the same authority the
sample path uses: shown unless the column is *known* sensitive (governance tag or
explicit policy), masked when there is no column context at all.

Shown-unless-known-sensitive, not default-mask, is deliberate: the cell comes
from the column the user aimed the monitor at, so it is the analogue of
`partial_unexpected_list`'s tested column. Default-masking it would make every
"your timestamp column has junk in it" error unactionable, which is the failure
mode option (a) was rejected for.

The `sample_failures` retention/PII bypass on the errored branch was the load
bearing detail: that branch deliberately skips the PII path on the assumption
error messages carry no data. This one did.

Tests assert on the PERSISTED text, not on the exception, because the failure
mode is a value reaching a sink. Mutation-verified both directions: forcing
`show = True` reds 3 tests; putting the value back in the message reds 1.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
